en.title: Netflix Offered 'Obsession' a Straight-to-Streaming Deal, Director Reveals
en.summary: Director Curry Barker disclosed that Netflix made a bold offer to acquire his breakout horror hit 'Obsession' for a direct-to-streaming release. This offer came before the film's successful theatrical run and bidding war among major studios.
en.body:
## The Path Not Taken: Netflix's Streaming Bid for 'Obsession'

In a fascinating glimpse behind the curtain of Hollywood deal-making, **Curry Barker**, the visionary director behind the critically acclaimed romantic horror film **Obsession**, has revealed that **Netflix** once offered to take his breakout hit straight to streaming. This surprising offer emerged after **Obsession** premiered to rave reviews at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), a moment that unexpectedly ignited a fierce bidding war among major distributors.

Barker recounted waking up the morning after the TIFF premiere to a barrage of missed calls from his manager, agent, and the film's financier, signaling a seismic shift in the film's trajectory. "You name it, every company. Neon, Focus, A24, all of these companies are wanting to do your movie," Barker recalled, detailing the intense competition for his project. Among the interested parties was Netflix, which presented a unique proposition: bypass the theatrical window entirely and launch **Obsession** directly onto its global streaming platform. This offer stands in stark contrast to the film's eventual distribution through Focus Features, which led to its impressive box office performance and critical acclaim.

## The Streaming vs. Theatrical Debate

Barker's revelation offers a compelling "what if" scenario for fans who have embraced **Obsession** as a cinematic success story. The decision to pursue a theatrical release, rather than accepting Netflix's lucrative streaming offer, undoubtedly played a crucial role in the film's eventual status as a record-setter for its budget-to-box office ratio. It also raises questions about the long-term impact of streaming-first releases on a film's cultural resonance and its ability to generate widespread discussion and critical analysis beyond its initial release window. For dedicated series and film fans, this insight underscores the complex decisions directors face in navigating the evolving landscape of content distribution and the potential trade-offs between immediate financial gain and lasting artistic legacy.

## What's Next for Curry Barker

While details about **Curry Barker**'s upcoming projects have not yet been fully announced, his success with **Obsession** has firmly established him as a director to watch. Fans eager to see his next move can anticipate further announcements regarding his future endeavors in film and television.

content_raw: Today, in “Boy, you kind of dodged a bullet there” news: Curry Barker has revealed that his breakout horror hit Obsession   could have been the latest movie to get briefly tossed on the very tippy-top of Netflix’s endlessly churning vat of entertainment quicksand, before ultimately sinking into the mire. Instead of, you know, becoming the tenth-highest grossing film of 2026 to date, and a record-setter for the jump from a film’s budget to its ultimate box office take . Sliding Doors , huh? This is per  The Playlist , reporting on an interview Barker gave to the CBC this week in which he reflected on the reception his romantic horror film got after debuting at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025. Barker says he woke up the morning after the premiere to multiple missed calls from his manager, agent, and the film’s financier, letting him know he now had the happy problem of being in the middle of a bidding war. “You name it,” Barker recalls them telling him. “You know, every company. Neon, Focus, A24, all of these companies are wanting to do your movie.” That included Netflix, which “was in the conversation at one point. They put in an offer to just put it straight on Netflix.” Which is a genuinely interesting counterfactual to consider! It’s easy to imagine, after all, a universe where Barker took that offer, accepted a decent-sized pile of cash upfront, and let Netflix make a meal of his movie for the week or so it would take for the algorithm to churn and digest it. (It was, after all, not actually the first film he’d been invited to develop, as he was beginning his rise from his self-funded YouTube movie maker ranks; he’d actually been approached first, he notes in the interview, for a feature-length expansion of his online horror short The Chair .) (Which might still happen, by the way.) And it’s totally possible the film still would have caught on big—it succeeded in theaters because it grabbed people, hard, and it’s not like Netflix success stories like Kpop Demon Hunters  don’t exist. But it still makes you wonder things like, “Would Disney have just announced it was going all-in on star Inde Navarrette as the X-Men’s new Rogue if she was the star of a well-received Netflix movie, instead of one of the defining elements of the biggest unlikely movie success of the year?” We’ll never know, of course, since Barker turned down the offer; he, and Focus Features, wound up reaping huge benefits from his decision to bet on theaters, instead.
